summary:
Same-sex relations are illegal in Eswatini for men and women throughout the country, as recorded on 12 March 2026. Legal gender recognition is not available, so a trans visitor's documents will be read as issued, and no route exists to align them with lived gender.

LGBTI organisations cannot register in Eswatini. The registrar of companies refused registration to an LGBTI group in July 2019, and the government continues to deny such groups organisational status. A visitor should not expect to find a registered national advocacy body to contact for assistance.

Hostility from official figures is on the record. A 2021 United States State Department report found that some traditional, religious and government officials publicly criticised same-sex sexual conduct as neither locally nor Christian in character.

Public visibility nonetheless exists and has been tolerated in narrow form. The first Eswatini Pride was held in July 2018 and described as a success, and in June 2021 LGBTQI+ people held a virtual Pride celebration without incident. These events mark a small space of visibility in a state where the underlying conduct remains criminal.

The wider environment is an absolute monarchy with severely restricted civic space, which shapes how any incident involving a trans visitor would be handled by authorities.
tangentialFactors:
Freedom in the World 2024 rates Eswatini Not Free with an overall score of 17 out of 100, comprising 1 out of 40 for political rights and 16 out of 60 for civil liberties. The rating reflects an absolute monarchy with severely restricted civic space rather than a targeted assessment of LGBT conditions, but it indicates the weakness of redress mechanisms generally.

The BTI 2024 country report places the refusal to register LGBTQ+ groups inside a broader pattern of restricted political formations, meetings and recruitment, describing an oppressive environment in which the slogan calling for the monarch's departure has become common at protests. Organisational bans in Eswatini are therefore not confined to LGBT groups.

Religious inclusion is uneven rather than absent. A church welcoming LGBTIQ people reopened in December 2018, documented alongside a continuing absence of let-up in discrimination in the kingdom.
localsOnly:
Registration of an LGBTI organisation is refused at administrative level. The registrar of companies turned down an LGBTI group's application in July 2019, and BTI 2024 records that the government denies LGBTQ+ groups the ability to register as organisations.

Eswatini Pride has run since the inaugural event declared a success in July 2018, with a virtual celebration held in June 2021 without incident. Organisers operate under the constraint that the underlying conduct remains criminal.

A welcoming church reopened in December 2018, giving LGBTIQ people at least one documented religious space, while Swazi Media Commentary recorded that discrimination in the kingdom showed no let-up at the time.

Traditional, religious and government officials have publicly criticised same-sex conduct as neither locally nor Christian, which residents may encounter in official and community settings.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state the penalty, statute or enforcement record for same-sex relations in Eswatini, only that the conduct is illegal for men and women as of 12 March 2026. The specific legal provision and any arrests remain unresolved on this evidence.

No sourced material in this inventory addresses access to trans-specific healthcare, hate-crime or non-discrimination protection, partner or marriage recognition, detention or prison placement rules, or entry, visa and border-screening treatment of trans travellers. Any statement on those points would be unsourced here.

The scope of legal gender recognition is recorded only as unavailable; whether any administrative or court route exists in practice, and whether foreign documents are accepted for accommodation or hotel registration, is not covered.

The 2021 official criticism and the 2021 virtual Pride come from a single reporting year, and the inventory does not establish whether that pattern of official comment has continued since.
